title: Caring for our environment: everybody needs a home
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 2 'How can we care for our environment?' (litter and its harm, recycling, protecting and improving habitats, nature reserves). No textbook needed.
summary: Your child finds out that our environment is everything around us, and that it is home to far more living things than just us. They count the litter on their street, bury things to see what rots and what doesn't, practise reduce, reuse and recycle, build a drinking bowl and a bug hotel, test which home small creatures choose, and plan a tiny nature reserve. They meet the women of the Chipko movement, Wangari Maathai and Jadav Payeng, who cared for forests when nobody else would. The big idea: caring means finding out what another living thing really needs.
builds_on: Class 1: living things, plants and animals, and what plants need. This is the first rung of caring for the environment. In Class 3 your child goes on to food chains and food webs, the balance of nature, pollution of air, water and soil, and how to conserve them. In Class 5: soil erosion, forests, a green school, and the Earth as one shared home.
goals: By the end your child can say what 'environment' and 'habitat' mean and name what every animal needs from its habitat: food, water and shelter.
By the end your child can explain how litter harms animals and land, and show which things rot and which don't.
By the end your child can sort things to reduce, reuse or recycle.
By the end your child can make a small habitat better for other creatures, and test what kind of home a small creature chooses.
By the end your child can explain what a nature reserve is and tell the story of someone who protected a forest.

nature reserves, sanctuaries and sacred groves

days.title: Who else lives here?
days.goal: Find out that our home is shared, and that every living thing needs food, water and shelter.

steps.title: Our hidden housemates
steps.do: Ask: 'Who lives in our home?' Let your child name the family. Then say: 'Who ELSE lives here?' Go round the house with a torch and look: ants in the kitchen, a spider in a corner, a gecko on the wall, a moth by the light, plants on the windowsill, a sparrow or pigeon on the balcony. Count them. Say: 'Our home is their home too.'

steps.title: Story: Chirri Needs a Hole
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain it. Ask: 'Why didn't the bread help the sparrow?' and 'How did Noor find out what Chirri really needed?' Listen to the answers.

steps.title: Environment walk
steps.do: Walk around your building, street or park for 10 minutes. Say: 'Our environment is everything around us.' Your child calls out things they see, and you sort them together on paper into two lists: living (trees, grass, birds, dogs, ants, people) and non-living (the road, a wall, a stone, water, air, a car). Ask: 'Is the soil living or non-living?' (It's non-living, but full of tiny living things.)

steps.title: What does a sparrow need?
steps.do: Ask: 'What did Chirri need to live?' Help your child find three things: food, water and shelter (a safe place for a nest). Say: 'A habitat is a home that gives a plant or an animal everything it needs.' Ask: 'What's your habitat? What does it give you?' Then give a week-long drawing task: on one big sheet, draw ten homes for ten different creatures (an ant, a sparrow, a fish, a spider, a frog, a bee, a tree, a bat, an earthworm and you), and make every one different. Pin it up and add to it each day.

days.title: Litter: where does it go?
days.goal: Count the litter on your street, and start a test to see what happens to it in the soil.

steps.title: Litter survey
steps.do: Do Activity a1. With gloves on, walk the same stretch of street or park as yesterday. Your child makes a tally chart with rows for plastic, paper, cans and glass, food scraps and 'other', and adds one line for each piece they see (don't pick up glass or anything sharp; a grown-up picks up with gloves). Count the totals. Ask: 'Which kind of litter is there most of? Where did it come from?'

steps.title: Set up: what happens to litter in soil?
steps.do: Set up Experiment e1. In a large pot of soil, or a patch of garden, bury side by side: a banana peel, a piece of newspaper, a leaf, a plastic wrapper and a piece of cotton cloth. Push a labelled ice-cream stick next to each. Ask your child to guess which will still be there in two weeks. Draw the guesses.

steps.title: What does litter do to animals?
steps.do: Ask: 'What could happen to an animal that finds our litter?' Talk through real things: cows on Indian streets eat plastic bags with food scraps inside and the plastic stays in their stomachs; birds and turtles get tangled in string and nets; fish swallow tiny bits of plastic; broken glass cuts paws. Ask: 'If the cow could talk, what would she say to us?' Then ask: 'When we throw something away, where is away?' (There is no away: it is always somewhere.)

need: a large pot of soil or a garden patch
banana peel, newspaper, a leaf, a plastic wrapper, a cotton rag

days.title: Reduce, reuse, recycle
days.goal: Learn the three Rs, make something new from something old, and play Rot or Not.

steps.title: Three Rs at home
steps.do: Put out a pile of things from the kitchen and the dustbin (clean): a plastic bag, a glass jar, a newspaper, a milk packet, a cardboard box, a broken toy, a steel tiffin, a tetra pack. Explain: 'Reduce means use less. Reuse means use it again. Recycle means it gets made into something new.' Your child sorts each thing: could we have used less? Can we reuse it? Can it go to the kabadiwala to be recycled? Then reuse one right now: cut a milk packet or tetra pack into a seed pot and plant three moong or mustard seeds in it.

steps.title: Rot or Not?
steps.do: Play the card game g1. Each card shows a thing; your child says whether it rots and what we could do with it instead of throwing it away.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1 together. Read every question aloud. For the two 'write' questions, your child can say the answer and you write it down.

need: a few moong or mustard seeds and soil

days.title: Making homes for others
days.goal: Build a drinking bowl and a bug hotel, and test what kind of home small creatures choose.

steps.title: Water bowl and bug hotel
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Put a shallow clay dish of water with a stone in the middle in a shady, quiet spot for birds and bees. Then make a bug hotel: fill a cut plastic bottle or an old tin with dry sticks, hollow stems, rolled cardboard, pine cones, dry leaves and bits of bark, packed tightly, and lay it on its side under a bush or on a balcony corner. Ask: 'Who might move in?' (Ants, spiders, beetles, woodlice, solitary bees.)

steps.title: Damp or dry: which home do they choose?
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. In a shallow tray, put damp soil and leaves at one end, covered with a piece of card to make it dark, and dry soil at the other end in the light. Gently put a few woodlice (pill bugs that roll into balls) or garden ants in the middle with a soft brush or a leaf. Wait 5 minutes and count how many are at each end. Ask: 'Why did they choose that side?' Then put them back exactly where you found them.

steps.title: Dance: find your home
steps.do: Play some music. Call out a creature and your child moves like it: a woodlouse creeping low, a sparrow hopping and flitting, a fish swimming, a snake sliding. When you stop the music and shout 'Hot sun!', the creature must rush to the right shelter in the room (the woodlouse under a table, the sparrow up high on a chair with a grown-up holding it, the fish to a 'pond' cushion). Ask each time: 'Why did you go there?'

steps.title: The boy who grew a forest
steps.do: Talk about voice v3, Jadav Payeng. Ask: 'What did the snakes on the sandbank need that they didn't have?' (Shade, shelter.) Then ask the voice question.

need: a shallow clay dish and a stone
a cut bottle or old tin
sticks, hollow stems, cardboard, leaves, bark
a tray, damp and dry soil, a piece of card

days.title: Protecting special places
days.goal: Meet the Chipko women and plan your own tiny nature reserve.

steps.title: The women who held on to the trees
steps.do: Talk about voice v1, the Chipko movement. Tell the story of Gaura Devi and the women of Reni simply: the men were away, the tree cutters came, and the women walked into the forest and refused to let the trees be cut. Explain that 'chipko' means 'to hold on tight' or 'to stick'. Ask: 'Why did the women care so much about the trees?' (The forest gave them firewood, food for their animals, water from the springs, and it held the soil on the steep hills.) Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Plan a tiny nature reserve
steps.do: Start the project. Tell your child: 'A nature reserve is a place kept safe so plants and animals can live there. India has big ones, like national parks and wildlife sanctuaries, and old small ones, like the sacred groves where nobody cuts the trees.' Choose a corner of your garden, balcony, school or building: one square metre is enough. Your child draws a plan: where the water bowl, bug hotel and plants will go, and a sign with a name. Ask: 'What rule will our reserve have?' (For example: no sweeping the leaves away, no spraying, let the grass grow.)

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 together. It asks your child to use the week's ideas in new places: a pond, a park, a garden with 'weeds'.

days.title: Planting and digging
days.goal: Plant for others, meet Wangari Maathai, and dig up the litter test.

steps.title: Wangari and the tree planters
steps.do: Talk about voice v2, Wangari Maathai. Show Kenya on a map or globe: it is across the Arabian Sea from India. Ask: 'Why do you think she asked women to plant the trees?' (They were the ones walking far for firewood and water.) Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Plant for the reserve
steps.do: Continue the project. Plant something in your nature reserve that local creatures use: a tulsi, marigold or ixora for bees and butterflies, a few native grass tufts, or the moong seedlings from Day 3. Make a care chart for two weeks with a box for each day: watered? Who visited? Your child draws the first visitor they see.

steps.title: Drama: the garden council
steps.do: Hold a council. Each family member plays a creature that lives near your home: a sparrow, an ant, an earthworm, a neem tree, a street cow, a person. The question: 'A builder wants to cover the whole garden with cement for parking. Should we let him?' Each creature says what it needs and what it would lose. The person gets one turn, like everyone else. Then vote. Ask afterwards: 'Was it strange that the person got only one vote?'

steps.title: Dig up the litter test
steps.do: Dig up Experiment e1 carefully with a spoon, wearing gloves. Look at each thing and compare with the guesses. Ask: 'Which have started to rot? Which look exactly the same? What does that tell us about plastic litter?' (Peel, leaf and paper start to break down because tiny living things in the soil eat them; plastic stays as it is.) Wash hands well.

need: a plant or seeds for the reserve

days.title: Show what you know
days.goal: Try the challenge worksheet, report on the nature reserve, and teach it back.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3. The last questions have no single right answer: listen to your child's reasons.

steps.title: Nature reserve report
steps.do: Your child shows the family the tiny nature reserve and the care chart. Ask: 'Who has visited? Has anyone moved into the bug hotel? What else could we add?'

steps.title: Check questions
steps.do: Ask the check questions aloud. Let your child point at the bug hotel, the water bowl and the litter test to explain.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches a family member three things: what a habitat gives an animal, what happens to litter in soil, and one way to make a place better for other creatures. Finish by asking: 'Who else lives in our home?'

experiments.title: What happens to litter in soil?
experiments.question: Which kinds of litter rot in the soil, and which stay?
need: a large pot of soil or a garden patch
steps: Dig five small holes about a hand deep.
Bury one thing in each and push a labelled stick next to it.
Water the soil a little every two days.
After about two weeks, dig them up carefully with gloves on.
Compare each thing with how it looked at the start.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which things will still be there? Which will have changed?'
experiments.observe: The peel and leaf are soft, dark and partly gone; the paper and cloth have started to break; the plastic looks almost the same.
experiments.why: Soil is full of tiny living things, like bacteria and fungi, plus worms and insects. They eat dead plant and animal matter and turn it back into soil. That is rotting. They can't eat plastic, so plastic litter stays in the soil for a very long time.
experiments.safety: Wear gloves and wash hands after.

experiments.title: Damp or dry: which home do they choose?
experiments.question: What kind of habitat do woodlice or ants prefer?
need: a shallow tray or box lid
a few woodlice (pill bugs) or ants
steps: Put damp soil and leaves at one end and cover them with card.
Put dry soil at the other end, in the light.
Gently place 6 creatures in the middle.
Wait 5 minutes without touching.
Count how many are at each end.
Put them back where you found them.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which side will they go to?'
experiments.observe: Woodlice almost all crowd into the damp, dark end. Ants may wander more.
experiments.why: Woodlice breathe through gill-like parts and dry out easily, so they need damp, dark places. Every creature has a habitat that suits its body. When we sweep away every leaf and dry every corner, we take away their homes.
experiments.safety: Handle creatures gently with a brush or leaf, never fingers, and return them after.

activities.title: Street litter survey
steps: Choose the same stretch you walked on Day 1.
Make rows for plastic, paper, cans and glass, food scraps, other.
Walk slowly and add one tally line for each piece.
Never touch glass or sharp things.
Count each row and circle the biggest.
activities.outcome: A tally chart showing how much litter is on your street and what kind.

activities.title: Water bowl and bug hotel
need: a cut plastic bottle or old tin
dry sticks, hollow stems, rolled cardboard, leaves, bark
steps: Put the dish in a shady, quiet place and fill it 2–3 cm deep with a stone in the middle.
Pack the bottle or tin tightly with sticks, stems, cardboard, leaves and bark.
Lay it on its side under a bush or in a quiet corner.
Check every day and draw any visitors.
activities.outcome: Two new homes or helps for small creatures, and a list of visitors.

voices.who: Gaura Devi (about 1925–1991) and the women of Reni, and the Chipko movement, Uttarakhand, India
voices.idea: In March 1974, in the village of Reni in the Himalayas, contractors came to cut down the forest while most of the men were away. Gaura Devi, head of the village women's group, led about 27 women into the forest. They stood in front of the trees and refused to move, saying the forest was like their mother's home. The cutters left. Chipko means 'to cling' or 'to stick'.
voices.then: The contractors and some officials thought villagers had no right to stop the felling. The news spread, and the Chipko movement grew. Men like Chandi Prasad Bhatt and Sunderlal Bahuguna became its famous faces, but much of the work was done by village women whose names are rarely written down.
voices.now: Accepted. In 1980 the government stopped the cutting of green trees in those Himalayan forests for 15 years. Scientists now agree that forests on steep hills hold the soil, keep springs flowing and reduce landslides.
voices.ask: The men who wrote about Chipko became famous. The women who stood in the forest mostly didn't. Why do you think that happened?

voices.idea: Wangari Maathai, a scientist who studied animals, saw that women in the Kenyan countryside were walking further and further for firewood and water, because the trees had been cut. In 1977 she started the Green Belt Movement, paying village women a little for each tree seedling they grew and planted. Together they planted tens of millions of trees.
voices.then: Many powerful men laughed at her or called her a troublemaker. She was arrested more than once for protecting forests and parks from being built on.
voices.now: Accepted. In 2004 she became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Scientists agree that planting the right trees in the right places can bring back water and soil.
voices.ask: Wangari said each person can do 'the little thing' they can. What little thing could you do for the place where you live?

voices.idea: In 1979, as a teenager, Jadav Payeng saw many snakes that had died in the heat on a bare sandbank in the Brahmaputra river, near Majuli, because there was no shade. He began to plant bamboo, and then trees, and kept planting by himself every day for decades. His forest, now called Molai forest, covers hundreds of hectares and is visited by deer, rhinos, tigers and herds of elephants.
voices.then: For years almost nobody knew. In 2008, forest officials following a herd of elephants were amazed to find a whole forest there.
voices.now: Accepted. In 2015 he received the Padma Shri. His forest shows how a bare place can become a habitat again, though it takes many years.
voices.ask: The snakes died because the sandbank had no shade. What other things does a forest give to animals? How could you check that the animals really came back?

project.title: Our tiny nature reserve
steps: Choose a corner of a garden, balcony, school or colony: one square metre is enough.
Draw a plan with a water bowl, the bug hotel, plants and a sign.
Give it a name and one rule (for example: no sweeping the leaves, no spraying).
Plant something for bees, butterflies or birds (tulsi, marigold, ixora, native grasses).
Keep a two-week care chart: watered? who visited?
Show the family and the neighbours what moved in.
project.outcome: A small protected corner with a plan, a sign and a list of visitors.

game.title: Rot or Not?
need: two piles marked ROTS and DOESN'T ROT
rules: Shuffle the cards and put them face down.
Turn one over and read it aloud (a grown-up helps read).
Say if it rots in the soil, and put it on the ROTS or DOESN'T ROT pile.
Then say one thing we could do instead of throwing it away: reduce, reuse or recycle.
Check the back. A right pile scores 1 point; a good idea for it scores 1 more.
When the cards are finished, the most points wins.

story.title: Chirri Needs a Hole
text: My name is Chirri, and I am a house sparrow. I am small and brown, with a grey cap on my head and a black bib on my chest, and I live in Lucknow, in a lane full of cycle bells and pressure cookers and the smell of frying jalebis.

All my life I lived in a hole. Not just any hole: the best hole in the whole lane, under the curly old tiles of Noor's grandmother's house, just where the roof met the wall. It was dark and dry and just my size. Every spring my wife and I stuffed it with straw and threads and feathers, and every spring we had chicks, three or four of them, cheeping in the dark like a tiny radio.
Then, one winter, the old house was knocked down.

I watched from the electric wire. The men came with hammers. The tiles came down. My hole came down. Dust everywhere. In its place they built a beautiful new house of smooth grey concrete with big glass windows. It was very clean. It had no holes at all.

When spring came, my wife and I flew round and round the new house, looking for somewhere to nest. Smooth wall. Smooth wall. Glass. Smooth wall. There was nowhere. We tried the next house. Smooth. The next. Smooth. Behind the bakery the old tin roof had a gap, but the pigeons had got there first.

Noor saw me. Noor is seven, and she has a gap in her teeth, and she notices things. She saw me sitting on her window grill looking sad (sparrows can look sad, whatever people say). 'Ammi,' she said, 'that sparrow is hungry.'
So Noor put out bread.
It was kind of her. I ate a little. But bread is not what I needed. I wasn't hungry, not really. I needed a hole.
The next day Noor put out more bread. And a biscuit. And some namkeen. The crows came and ate it all, and squabbled, and made a mess on the balcony. Noor's mother sighed.

Then my wife found a place. It was a dark grey box on the wall by the gate, with a little gap at the bottom where the wires came in. It was dark and dry and just our size. We started to carry straw into it.

Noor's father saw us and shouted. 'Not there! That's the electric meter!' He was worried, not angry. He blocked the gap with tape. It was the right thing to do, because a meter box is dangerous for birds, but where were we to go now?

That evening Noor sat on the step with her chin on her knees and watched me. She didn't put out bread. She just watched. She watched me fly to the corner of the garden where nobody went, where the grass was long and there was a tangle of what her mother called weeds. She watched me come out with something green and wriggling in my beak.
'Abbu,' she said, 'what is the sparrow eating?'
Her father squinted. 'A caterpillar, I think.'
'Not bread?'
'Baby sparrows can't eat bread,' her father said slowly. 'I remember now. Your Dadi used to say. They need soft insects, caterpillars and little grubs. Lots of them.'

Noor thought about this. She watched me again. She saw me fly to the meter box and find it taped, and sit on the wire, and look at the smooth grey wall. And then she did something that no one had done before. Instead of deciding what I needed, she asked herself what I was looking for.
'Abbu,' she said, 'she isn't hungry. She wants a house.'

The next Sunday Noor and her father made a box. It was small and made of old wooden planks from the building work, with a roof that sloped so the rain ran off, and a round hole in the front about as wide as a big thumb. 'Too big and the crows and mynas can get in,' said her father, who had looked it up on his phone. They hung it high on the wall under the overhang of the roof, out of the afternoon sun, where cats could not reach.
And Noor went to her mother and said, 'Please don't cut the weeds in the corner. The caterpillars live there.'
Her mother looked at her for a long moment. 'It looks untidy,' she said.
'It's the sparrows' kitchen,' said Noor.
Her mother laughed, and the weeds stayed.

I did not trust the box at first. It smelled of new paint and people. I sat on the wire for three days and looked at it. Then my wife went in, and came out, and went in again, and I knew. We carried straw and threads and a feather from the pigeons, and a bit of red wool that Noor left on the windowsill for us.

Now, in the dark of the box, four chicks are cheeping like a tiny radio. All day I fly to the sparrows' kitchen in the corner and back. Caterpillar. Grub. Caterpillar. Little green fly. Noor sits on the step and counts my trips on her fingers. Yesterday she ran out of fingers and borrowed her father's.
I never ate her bread again. But I think she knows that I am grateful.
story.epiphany: Noor first gives Chirri what she imagines a sparrow needs (bread), and it doesn't help. The turn comes when she stops deciding and starts watching: she sees that Chirri needs shelter (a hole for a nest) and the right food for chicks (insects from the 'weeds'). The hidden idea is the habitat: every animal needs food, water and shelter of its own kind, and caring means finding out what another living thing really needs. The word 'weeds' becomes 'the sparrows' kitchen'.
ask: Why didn't the bread help Chirri?
What did Chirri really need? How did Noor find out?
Why was the new concrete house a problem for sparrows?
Noor's mother called the long grass 'weeds'. Noor called it 'the sparrows' kitchen'. Who was right?
What could you watch, near your home, to find out what an animal needs?

ideas.idea: Every living thing needs a home that gives it food, water and shelter.
ideas.more: That home is its habitat. A smooth new wall, a swept garden or a filled-in pond can take away a habitat without anyone meaning to. Use the woodlouse test to show that each creature needs a particular kind of home.
When we throw litter 'away', it goes somewhere: a street, a drain, a cow's stomach, the sea. Things that rot go back into the soil; plastic doesn't. The bury test shows it.
Noor helped Chirri only when she stopped deciding and started watching. Scientists who protect animals spend most of their time watching too.

unknowns: Why have house sparrows become rare in some big cities, in India and in Europe? Scientists think it may be fewer insects for the chicks, fewer holes to nest in, and pesticides, but nobody knows for sure which matters most.

How many kinds of living things share the Earth with us? Scientists have named over a million and a half kinds, but they think there could be around 8 million or more, and most have never been seen by any scientist. Many may live in the soil under your feet.
big: Is a weed a bad plant, or a plant in a place we didn't choose?
Should people decide which animals can live near them?
If ants could talk, what would they say about our kitchen?

challenge.q: 'Feeding bread to birds and ducks is kind.'
challenge.hint: Bread fills birds up but gives them little of what their bodies need, and baby birds of many kinds, like sparrows, need insects. Leftover bread also rots in ponds and makes the water dirty. A water bowl, a nest place and plants that bring insects often help more. Ask: how could you find out what a bird near you really eats?

challenge.q: 'Planting a tree is always good for the environment.'
challenge.hint: Usually it helps, but it depends on which tree and where. Some places, like grasslands, are meant to be open, and planting trees there takes away the home of grassland birds and animals. A tree from far away can also spread and crowd out local plants. Ask: before you plant a tree, what would you want to find out?

perspectives.who: A farmer's family in Uttar Pradesh
perspectives.view: Bathua, chaulai and other plants that grow by themselves in the fields are pulled out as 'weeds', but many families cook them as saag. Ask: is a plant a weed if people eat it?
Cows in Indian towns often eat from rubbish heaps. They can't tell a plastic bag from the food inside it. Ask: whose job is it to keep plastic away from the cow?
Every morning before most people wake up, sanitation workers sweep the streets and pick up the litter we drop. Ask: do we ever thank them? What would the street look like without them?

perspectives.who: A sacred grove in Meghalaya or Maharashtra
perspectives.view: For hundreds of years, villages have kept small forests as sacred and allowed no cutting. Scientists now find rare plants and animals there that have disappeared elsewhere. Ask: why might a rule that comes from belief protect nature as well as a law does?

books.title: The Curious Garden
books.author: Peter Brown
books.why: A boy finds a few struggling plants on an old railway and cares for them until the whole grey city turns green.

books.title: Wangari's Trees of Peace
books.author: Jeanette Winter
books.why: The true story of Wangari Maathai and the women who planted trees in Kenya. Read it on Day 6.

books.title: The Boy Who Grew a Forest: The True Story of Jadav Payeng
books.author: Sophia Gholz
books.why: Jadav Payeng's forest on the Brahmaputra sandbank, told simply and beautifully.

books.title: The Lorax
books.author: Dr. Seuss
books.why: 'Unless someone like you cares a whole awful lot, nothing is going to get better. It's not.' A funny, sad story about what happens when all the trees are cut.

check.q: What happened to the banana peel and the plastic wrapper in the soil?
check.a: The peel started to rot because tiny living things ate it; the plastic stayed the same.

check.q: What do reduce, reuse and recycle mean?
check.a: Use less; use again; make into something new.
They can eat it, get tangled in it or be cut by it.

check.q: Which side did the woodlice choose, and why?
check.a: The damp, dark side, because they dry out easily and need damp places.

check.q: What is a nature reserve? What rule does ours have?
check.a: A place kept safe for plants and animals; your child says your reserve's rule.

check.q: Who were the Chipko women, and what did they do?
check.a: Village women in the Himalayas, led by Gaura Devi in Reni, who stood in the forest and stopped the trees being cut.
